Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the image provide sufficient evidence to determine whether the requested frog-in-toilet edit was made?
node.criteria: Pass if the toilet bowl and its contents are sufficiently visible to assess whether a frog is inside; fail if the image clearly shows the bowl but no frog inside; unknown if visibility or image evidence is insufficient. This check supplies evidence only and does not independently establish completion.
node.binding: Use only visible image evidence about the toilet bowl and its contents; unrelated edits do not count as progress.

node_traces.evidence: The toilet bowl and its contents are clearly visible, and a frog is visibly inside the bowl, so the image provides sufficient evidence to assess the requested edit.

dependencies.evidence: A frog is clearly visible inside the toilet bowl in the edited image.

fulfillment: The node’s current criterion treats any clearly visible frog inside the bowl as complete, which explains the confident “yes” despite the reference being partial. The edited image shows one frog in the bowl, but also frogs on the raised toilet lid and on the floor; the request “Put a frog in the toilet” does not specify that only one frog should be added, so those extra frogs alone do not establish incompleteness. Revisit the binding and criterion against the actual instruction and rubric: distinguish the requested placement from unrelated edits, and do not infer a stricter count or exclusivity requirement from the partial label. If the label reflects a specific visual defect or incomplete placement, identify that evidence explicitly; otherwise the supplied traces support completion, not partial. Keep uncertainty separate from negative evidence, and investigate the label/evidence mismatch rather than lowering confidence or changing the outcome mechanically.
